figures.caption: Figure 1: UAV-viewpoint reference sampling and two-stage cross-domain retriever adaptation. Upper left: the CesiumJS-based sampler places virtual cameras over the 3D Tiles scene while varying (a) flight altitude, (b) horizontal grid interval, and (c) camera orientation, parameterised by yaw, pitch, and roll. Bottom left: Stage 1 constructs pose-near easy positives around real UAV poses and adapts SALAD with a multi-similarity loss. Upper right: self-distillation anchors the Stage-1 student to the pre-trained SALAD teacher. Bottom right: Stage 2 mines geographically distant look-alikes under the Stage-1 descriptor and suppresses them with a triplet loss.

Figure 4: Accuracy–speed–size Pareto view on Urbanscape. Each marker is one Ours∗ + matcher pipeline. Horizontal: per-query latency at K=5 from Table 7 (FP32, RTX 3090, log scale). Vertical: joint 5◦/5 m R@1 from Table 6. Marker area ∝ query-side parameter footprint; adjacent GMACs / TMACs label is the K=5 multiply-accumulate budget at 322×322, N=2000 keypoints. Green ring: PnP success = 100%; red ring: <100%. RIM (∼119 M params, ∼158 GMACs, 67.9 ms) sits at the upper-left of the fullsuccess cluster: fastest among the four full-success pipelines and more than 2× smaller in compute than the next competitor, within ∼ 3 pp of the decoupled DeDoDe teacher (∼ 339 GMACs) that we distil from. Dense matchers (ELoFTR ∼ 2 TMACs, RoMa ∼16 TMACs) sit one to two orders of magnitude further to the right.

Figure B.4: Qualitative cross-domain retrieval on Urbanscape query #3033 (black border). The remaining panels show the Top-1 reference tile returned by Ours∗ + RIM and by seven SOTA VPR baselines run on the same query at the same input resolution (322×322): the five methods that also appear in the main recall tables — SALAD [4], SelaVPR++ [29], EigenPlaces [26], CosPlace [24], AnyLoc [28] — plus two additional contemporary VPR baselines that we evaluated on the same cache for robustness, SelaVPR (T-PAMI’24) and CricaVPR (CVPR’24). Ours∗ + RIM retrieves a tile 12 m from the true UAV pose (green border, success), while every SOTA baseline returns a tile ≥ 74 m away (red borders, failures spanning 74–276 m). The bottom-right panel is the nearest 3D-Tiles ground-truth reference for context. All distances are 3D Euclidean in area-centred ECEF coordinates; For the methods shared with the main quantitative comparison, full-test ranking statistics are reported in Tables 2 and 3 and visualised in Fig. B.3; SelaVPR and CricaVPR are included here as additional qualitative controls.

Table 3: Recall@K (%) on the Chang’an Park benchmark, 3D Euclidean distance metric, on the 2,315-query construction-filtered set (matching Table D.1). Conventions follow Table 2; the planar (XY) counterpart is in Supplementary Appendix F.

Table 2: Recall@K (%) on the EPFL urban (Urbanscape) benchmark with the full 3D Euclidean distance metric at tolerance radii τ ∈ {25, 50}m. Best per column in bold, runner-up underlined. “∗” marks retrievers whose head has been retrained on our posenear UAV–reference pairs (Section 3.2); Game4Loc is evaluated zero-shot from the authors’ GTA-UAV weights, while the unstarred general-VPR rows use officially released weights. The planar (XY) counterpart is in Supplementary Appendix F.

Figure B.5: Qualitative effect of geometric re-ranking on Urbanscape. Each case shows the same query (leftmost column) with its “before re-rank” Top-K (upper row) – the retrievalonly order returned by Ours∗ – and the “after re-rank” Top-K (lower row) produced by the RANSAC-fundamental-matrix verifier that feeds on the RIM dense local descriptors. Green borders mark references within 25 m of the ground-truth UAV position, red borders mark references farther than 50 m. The top retrieval candidate is frequently a visually plausible but geometrically-off tile; once the RIM re-ranker runs, the correct tile is promoted to the first position in every case, which is what ultimately feeds PnP and produces the pose Recall gains reported in Table 6.

Table 4: Quantitative effect of geometric re-ranking on the Urbanscape test queries, under the same Ours∗ + RIM pipeline. The retrieval ranking is produced by the global descriptor; the re-ranked order is produced by the 2D–2D fundamental-matrix inlier count obtained with USAC-MAGSAC on the local descriptor matches (Section 3.4). The PnP inlier row is a downstream diagnostic measured on the selected Top-1.

Table 5: Top-K=5 geometric re-ranking on EPFL urban (R@1, %). Row 1 is Ours∗ retrieval only; remaining rows apply the indicated matcher on the same Top-5 candidate list. R@5 is identical to the retrieval-only row (74.16 / 94.87 at τ=25/50 m XY, 42.31 / 87.40 at τ=25/50 m 3D) since re-ranking only permutes the retrieved set. All matchers run at 322×322 with USAC-MAGSAC.

Table C.3: Decoder bridging ablation between the DINOv2-B (768 d) backbone and the DeDoDe descriptor decoder (1024 d). All four variants share the same Ours∗ retriever, USAC-MAGSAC verifier and PnP solver, evaluated on the 3,158-query Urbanscape test split at 322×322. “DeDoDe-G (no distill)” is the un-distilled teacher reference. The native-768 row is RIM’s adopted design.

Figure B.1: Generic retrieve-then-match-then-localise pipeline for cross-domain UAV global visual localization, of which virtually every prior system is an instance. The real UAV query Iq is encoded by a global retriever and matched against the reference database {Idb i }N i=1 by cosine similarity to produce Top-K candidates. A separate localfeature branch extracts descriptors for geometric re-ranking; database-side descriptors can be cached for sparse pipelines, whereas dense pairwise matchers run on every query– candidate pair. The resulting 2D–2D correspondences are verified by USAC-MAGSAC fundamental- matrix estimation, and the candidate with the largest inlier set is promoted to Top-1. Because the database pixels carry pixel-aligned ECEF coordinates (Section 3.2), the Top-1 2D–2D inlier set is lifted, in a single indexing step, to a 2D–3D correspondence set, and the final 6-DoF UAV pose is solved by RANSAC-PnP on area-centred ECEF coordinates (Section 3.5). A conventional sparse pipeline therefore uses separate global and local query encoders; a dense pairwise pipeline additionally repeats its matching network over the K candidates. Section 3.4 and Fig. 2 show how RIM removes the separate global DINOv2 query encoding by sharing one DINOv2-B representation between the two branches.

Table 6: End-to-end pose estimation on Urbanscape (Nq=3,158 test queries, 322×322, USAC-MAGSAC at 3 px). All pipelines share the same Ours∗ retriever followed by the indicated matcher. “Succ.” is the PnP success rate; the PnP R@1 and Joint 5◦/5 m R@1 columns are normalised over all Nq queries (PnP failures count as mis-localisations); median translation and rotation errors are reported over successful queries only. RIM runs retriever and matcher in one shared forward pass; DeDoDe (separate) uses two.

Table D.2: Joint 5 m/5◦ R@1 (%) on Park as a function of simulated barometric altitude precision σb (m). σb≤10 m is satisfied by any consumer-grade UAV barometer; σb =50 m is a no-information control. A σb = 10 m prior already delivers a 2× improvement on the strongest matcher, while σb = 1 m delivers a near-uniform ∼ 5× across every matcher — the signature of a single shared geometric bottleneck (nadir PnP vertical observability) at the 5 m position threshold.

Figure 2: Overview of the Retrieval-In-Matching (RIM) framework. Left: a schematic of related jointly optimised global–local architectures, in which the shared feature extractor and the detector, local-descriptor, and global-aggregation heads are trained together. Middle: adaptation of the RIM local branch by knowledge distillation. The frozen DeDoDeG teacher supplies dense local-descriptor targets; the cross-domain-adapted DINOv2-B backbone, global aggregation head, detector, and VGG19 stream are fixed, and only the student descriptor decoder is optimised. Right: RIM inference. One shared DINOv2-B backbone forward supplies the token field FB to the frozen global aggregation head and the distilled local-descriptor decoder. They produce the global descriptor g and dense local descriptor map D, respectively, while the detector provides keypoints K for local sampling, re-ranking, and pose estimation.

Figure B.2: Concrete samples drawn from the orthogonal fine-tuning dataset (UrbanscapeOOP, geographically disjoint from both test benchmarks; see Table 1). Left-edge colours encode the image source: black = real UAV, blue = 3D-Tiles rendering, red = mined hard negative. Source pairs: four real UAV queries paired with the nearest UAV-perspective renderings sampled from a photogrammetric 3D mesh via the grid protocol of Section 3.2 – the raw cross-domain material the fine-tuner has to align. Easy pair: one real UAV anchor followed by three renderings under bounded translation and orientation perturbations, kept as pose-near positives by the multi-similarity loss of Strategy 1. Hard triplet: two mined hard-negative triplets [anchor | positive | hard-negative]. The number reported above each triplet is the anchor-to-hard-negative cosine similarity (cos sim) and ∆ dist is the verified ECEF distance between the positive and the hard-negative. Both triplets are nearly indistinguishable to a visual retriever (cosine similarity ∼ 0.6 to the anchor) yet correspond to grid tiles separated by several hundred metres on the ground – exactly the failure mode Strategy 2 is designed to fix.

Figure 3: Cross-domain benchmark overview: two representative real UAV queries (black border) next to their nearest UAV-perspective reference tile (blue border) produced by the grid sampler of Section 3.2. Top, Urbanscape (EPFL): a piloted oblique flight vs. a nadir tile from a planned high-altitude grid, illustrating the large viewpoint variation a single photogrammetric mesh has to absorb. Bottom, Chang’an Park: a tree-lined avenue and a waterfront curve, illustrating the vegetation + water low-landmark regime where reference and queries are captured at least one year apart. The two benchmarks span qualitatively different axes of cross-domain difficulty (building clutter vs. vegetation, viewpoint shift vs. temporal drift).

Table D.1: Park ceiling decomposition (PUBLIC GT v4, N=2,315; full test set minus the 68 obvious new-construction frames whose mesh reference is invalid, cf. Section 4.1). Rotation R@5◦ is uniformly high while position R@5 m is the binding constraint of the joint metric. The rightmost column is the joint 5 m/5◦ Recall@1, which tracks the position channel since R@5◦ stays high.

Figure B.3: 3D Recall@1 at τ=25 m and τ=50 m for all competitors on the two benchmarks, plotted directly from Tables 2 and 3. Ours∗ (red) tops every competitor at both plotted tolerances on both benchmarks. NetVLAD(DINOv2)∗ is a matched-data finetuning baseline, while SelaVPR++ is shown in both released and same-data fine-tuned forms. Neither control reproduces the consistent gains of Ours∗, supporting an interaction between the SALAD aggregation head and the two-stage recipe rather than a generic benefit from exposure to the paired dataset.
